rationale: Scaffolding is a fair question for an agent framework like AutoGen, so the axis applies. The evidence shows only package installation via pip and AutoGen Studio, a visual drag-and-drop/JSON builder that can export teams to Python code. Neither is an official CLI command or project template that scaffolds a new agent project in one step.

Agent-oriented docs such as llms.txt or markdown docs are a fair axis for a developer framework like AutoGen, but the evidence shows no such offering. The llms.txt probe returned 404, and the markdown variant of the AgentChat user guide also returned 404. Confidence is medium rather than high because the llms.txt probe hit the microsoft.github.io root rather than the /autogen/ path.

AutoGen is an AI agent framework, so this axis applies. It can produce AI-generated analysis of user data only if you build it yourself: AssistantAgent pairs an LLM with tools, MagenticOneGroupChat targets open-ended web and file-based tasks, and AutoGen Studio offers an interactive environment for running agent teams. Nothing in the evidence shows a built-in, ready-made feature that surfaces insights or suggestions from your data. missing for 10: a turnkey in-product insights/suggestions feature over user data, documentation of data-connection and analysis workflows, independent hands-on evidence of insight quality.

AutoGen ships autonomous multi-agent execution primitives: programmatic `agent.run(task=...)`, team patterns (RoundRobin, Selector, Swarm, GraphFlow, MagenticOne), and AutoGen Studio options to export teams to Python, expose them as endpoints, or run them in a Docker container. Together these let a developer build autonomous workflows that could be deployed to run headlessly. However, background automation (scheduling, triggers, long-running daemons) is left to the user to build with external infrastructure. Missing for 10: built-in scheduling/cron or event triggers, documented background/daemon execution mode, monitoring of unattended runs, independent hands-on corroboration of background automation.

AutoGen ships a built-in AssistantAgent, an LLM-backed agent that can use tools, and you delegate work to it directly with `agent.run(task=...)`. AutoGen Studio adds an interactive environment for running agent teams, with pause and stop control. Missing for 10: a ready-to-use in-product assistant that needs no code or model-client setup, and independent hands-on corroboration that task delegation works well (the one community report on output quality is mixed).

AutoGen is a pip-installable Python framework whose agents and teams run programmatically with no UI, e.g. `await agent.run(task=...)`. Teams built in AutoGen Studio can be exported to Python code, exposed as endpoints, or run in a Docker container, so headless automation is clearly supported. Missing for 10: explicit CI/pipeline integration docs or examples, a documented headless CLI runner, and independent hands-on corroboration of CI usage.

AutoGen's official GitHub README shows an assistant agent that uses the Playwright MCP server. Combined with the documented tool-using AssistantAgent, this shows AutoGen can consume an external MCP server's tools. The evidence is a single README example, though, with no dedicated documentation of the MCP integration. Missing for 10: dedicated docs on MCP client setup (transports, configuration, connecting multiple servers), evidence it works with MCP servers beyond Playwright, independent or hands-on corroboration.

AutoGen is a multi-agent framework rather than an agent itself, so shipping an official MCP server is a fair question for it. The evidence only shows AutoGen agents consuming a third-party MCP server (Playwright) as a client. Nothing documents an official AutoGen MCP server or endpoint that external agents could connect to.

Agents and teams built with AutoGen accept natural-language tasks, for example `agent.run(task="Find information on AutoGen")`. MagenticOne handles open-ended tasks, UserProxyAgent lets a human give feedback to the team, and AutoGen Studio offers an interactive environment for running teams. However, setting up and operating the product itself is done through Python code, JSON specs or drag-and-drop, not natural-language commands. Missing for 10: natural-language configuration and building of agents and teams, an NL-driven CLI or control surface, independent hands-on corroboration of NL-only operation.

AutoGen is a multi-agent framework, so an official CLI is a fair question to ask of it. However, the evidence pack never documents one. It covers only pip installation of the Python packages, Python APIs such as agent.run, and AutoGen Studio, which is described as a visual drag-and-drop interface rather than a command-line tool.

AutoGen is a Python framework driven through a documented programmatic API. The docs show pip installation, AssistantAgent with `await agent.run(task=...)`, team classes (RoundRobinGroupChat, SelectorGroupChat, Swarm, GraphFlow), and component serialization, and AutoGen Studio adds exporting teams to Python and setting up endpoints from a team configuration. The OpenAPI probe 404s, which matters little for a library, but the evidence consists of user-guide snippets rather than a full API reference. missing for 10: an evidenced formal API reference, a documented HTTP API or OpenAPI spec for the Studio endpoints, and independent hands-on corroboration of driving it programmatically.

Per-agent credential scoping is a fair question for an agent framework, so the axis applies. However, nothing in the pack shows AutoGen issuing scoped or least-privilege API credentials to agents. The evidence covers agent types, team orchestration, AutoGen Studio and Docker code execution; none of it addresses credential scoping, and the probes found no API surface.

AutoGen is itself an official Microsoft Python SDK. It ships as pip-installable packages (`autogen-agentchat`, `autogen-ext[openai]`) with a documented programmatic API: `AssistantAgent`, `agent.run`, custom agents, and several team types (RoundRobin, Selector, Swarm, GraphFlow). Studio teams can also be exported to Python code. missing for 10: evidence of official SDKs beyond Python (no other language bindings shown), API-stability assurances (a 0.2→0.4 migration guide implies breaking changes, and the older `pyautogen` package name adds confusion), and independent hands-on corroboration of the current SDK.

AutoGen is a multi-agent framework with AutoGen Studio tooling, so outbound webhook event subscriptions are a plausible capability and the axis applies. The evidence covers logging of traces and setting up endpoints from team configurations, but nothing shows subscribing to events via webhooks, so the verdict is none.

The evidence shows code examples in the tutorial docs, such as the `agent.run(...)` snippet, and community users point to runnable example notebooks in the repo. AutoGen Studio offers an interactive environment for testing agent teams, but that is a team-building UI, not an API reference. Nothing shows an interactive API reference, and the probes found no OpenAPI spec. Missing for 10: an interactive/browsable API reference, examples runnable in-browser or inline in the reference, and first-party docs describing such a reference.

AutoGen is a framework whose AutoGen Studio can set up endpoints from team configurations, so a downloadable machine-readable API spec is a fair ask. However, no evidence shows an OpenAPI or equivalent spec being published. The JSON team specifications and component serialization describe agent configurations, not an API contract. The OpenAPI probe returned 404 on all candidate paths, but those paths were at the microsoft.github.io root rather than AutoGen-specific locations, so that check is weak.

AutoGen Studio offers an interactive environment for testing agent teams, can set up test endpoints, and can run teams in a Docker container. A community user reports that agent code execution runs in a fresh Docker container by default, which gives isolated sandbox execution. However, nothing in the evidence describes a sandbox that is explicitly separated from production data, or test or mock data environments. Missing for 10: documented sandbox-vs-production data separation, mock or test data tooling, first-party docs on Docker or isolated code executors, independent hands-on corroboration beyond one comment.

The evidence shows AutoGen has distinct versioned releases (0.2.x and 0.4.x), a 'stable' docs channel, and a published migration guide between major versions. Missing for 10: a documented deprecation policy, semantic-versioning or API-stability commitments, deprecation timelines or support windows, and independent corroboration.

Bulk or batch processing is a fair question for an agent-orchestration framework, so the axis applies. However, the evidence only documents single-task runs (agent.run), team configurations, and Studio run controls. Nothing describes batching, parallel fan-out, or acting on many items at once.

AutoGen's evidence shows only conversational routing that loosely resembles event-driven rules: Swarm agents hand off control via HandoffMessage, SelectorGroupChat uses a customizable selector to pick the next speaker after each message, and GraphFlow runs agents along a directed graph. AutoGen Studio can also expose teams as endpoints that external callers could invoke. None of this is documented as user-defined event→action rules, so support is glancing. Missing for 10: an explicit rule/trigger definition mechanism, external event sources (webhooks, schedules, file or system events), conditional edge or rule documentation, and hands-on corroboration.

Scheduling recurring runs is a fair question for an agent-workflow framework and its Studio tooling, so the axis applies. The evidence covers defining workflows (GraphFlow, teams), running them on demand, exposing endpoints and running them in Docker. Nothing shows built-in scheduling, cron-style triggers or recurring execution.

AutoGen has no built-in versioning, but the evidence makes automations portable artifacts that can be tracked in an external tool like git. Teams can be defined declaratively as JSON in AutoGen Studio, components can be serialized and deserialized, and teams can be exported as Python code. Review and rollback would rely entirely on outside tooling. Missing for 10: built-in version history, diff/review workflow for automation changes, one-click rollback to prior versions, and independent corroboration of a versioning workflow.

Checkpointing and resuming agent state is a fair question for a multi-agent framework like AutoGen, but the evidence pack never documents saving or loading agent or team state. The closest items are not about durable state: 'Serialize Components' covers component configuration, 'Memory' adds agent memory capabilities, and Studio's 'pause or stop execution' is run control. None of these show a run resuming exactly where it left off after a crash or restart.

The docs confirm that AssistantAgent is a built-in LLM agent that can use tools, and that running one is a single call (`agent.run(task=...)`) after a simple pip install. The GitHub README also shows agents using MCP-server tools and AgentTool. However, nothing in the pack shows how a developer defines a custom tool, such as a typed Python function with a type-hint-derived schema, or a concise end-to-end snippet. Durable execution is a fair question for an agent orchestration framework like AutoGen, but the pack shows no state checkpointing, resume-after-restart, or durable-execution integration. The closest items are component serialization (configuration, not runtime state), memory capabilities (context recall, not execution durability), and pause/stop run control in Studio. None of these shows agents surviving process restarts or deploys.

Evals and CI integration are a fair axis for an agent framework, but the pack has no evidence of built-in evals for scoring agent quality or of running evals in CI. The closest items are trace logging and AutoGen Studio's interactive testing environment and endpoint testing, which are manual testing and observability tools, not quality-scoring evals.

AutoGen agents and teams can be run programmatically from Python without a UI. The evidence shows `await agent.run(task=...)`, pip installation, exporting Studio teams to Python code, running teams in a Docker container, and logging traces, so a terminal script could execute and check agent output. However, nothing documents a headless CLI runner for the shipped example agents, and the community mention of examples refers to notebooks. Missing for 10: a documented terminal command or CLI for running example agents headlessly, machine-readable result output for automated verification, and hands-on corroboration of headless runs.

Missing for 10: documented conditional branching, loop/cycle support, parallel fan-out/fan-in steps, in-depth GraphFlow docs, and independent or hands-on corroboration.

Managing conversation history is a fair question for a multi-agent framework, so the axis applies. However, nothing in the pack describes trimming, summarizing, or filtering history to stay within a context window. The only nearby items are generic 'Add memory capabilities to your agents' lines, which concern memory stores rather than context-window history management, so they don't show this capability.

AutoGen Studio adds run control that can pause or stop execution, and a community user credits AutoGen with keeping the human in the loop to assist agents. Missing for 10: explicit evidence of approval-gating (approve/reject before an action proceeds), documented mechanics for resuming a paused run with the human's decision, and hands-on corroboration of mid-run pause/resume.

Input/output guardrails are a fair axis for a multi-agent framework like AutoGen, but the evidence pack never documents a guardrail, validator, or content-filtering hook for agent inputs or outputs. The nearby items do not cover this story: Docker-isolated code execution is sandboxing, and UserProxyAgent and custom agents are human feedback and general extensibility, not attachable guardrails that validate, transform, or block content.

AutoGen's AgentChat docs list a Memory section to "add memory capabilities to your agents," so the framework offers some agent memory. AutoGen Studio's docs say you can export and run teams in Python, set up and test endpoints from a team configuration, and run teams in a Docker container. Missing for 10: a vendor-managed or hosted runtime for deploying agents, detailed documentation of the endpoint/API surface (auth, scaling, invocation), and independent or hands-on corroboration of production endpoint deployment.

AutoGen documents human-in-the-loop support: the UserProxyAgent lets a human give feedback to the team, AutoGen Studio can pause or stop runs, and community users note it keeps a human in the loop. Agents can query databases through MCP or custom in-process tools, run parallel analyses with subagents, and return results as validated structured JSON. Users delegate a task through query(), and Claude evaluates it, calls tools and repeats until done, for example finding and fixing bugs without manual intervention. It can also spawn subagents for focused subtasks and pause for user approval or clarifying questions. Missing for 10: independent or hands-on corroboration that task delegation works as documented, since all supporting evidence is vendor docs.

The Agent SDK is a programmatic Python/TypeScript library built for unattended runs. Its docs describe agents that find and fix bugs "without manual intervention" and production hosting in Docker, Kubernetes and sandbox providers. Permission modes and rules define what runs automatically, structured outputs give machine-readable results, and a community user reports building a full headless automated workflow around `claude -p`. That puts it in the agent (MCP client) role, not the role of serving tools to other agents. Its MCP evidence covers only client-side use: connecting to local, HTTP, or in-process MCP servers to give its own agent tools. Nothing shows the SDK itself running as an official MCP server, such as an 'mcp serve' mode or a hosted endpoint, for outside agents to connect to. This is a judgment call: if the SDK were treated as a general framework rather than an agent, the verdict would be 'none'.
